title: DSA in Java: two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: Java versions of the window, stack and binary search patterns: ArrayDeque methods, overflow-safe midpoints, Arrays.binarySearch and the monotonic deque.
source: Oracle Java documentation (ArrayDeque, Deque, Arrays.binarySearch, Collections.binarySearch, java.util.Stack); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int maxArea(int[] h) for "container with most water": the bars at indices l and r hold min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l) water. Use two pointers starting at both ends.

checks.label: starts two pointers at the two ends and loops while l < r
computes the area with Math.min of the two heights
tracks the best with Math.max
moves a pointer inward each step
returns the best area

questions.explanation: Always move the shorter bar: moving the taller one can only shrink the width without raising the limiting height. Other loop shapes are fine if they are O(n).

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int lowerBound(int[] a, int x) returning the first index i with a[i] >= x in a sorted array (a.length if none). Use a half-open range [lo, hi).
questions.starter:
static int lowerBound(int[] a, int x) {

checks.label: uses a loop condition lo < hi
computes mid without overflow
moves lo to mid + 1 when a[mid] < x
sets hi = mid otherwise
returns lo

questions.explanation: The half-open range makes the loop invariant easy: everything left of lo is < x, everything from hi on is >= x. The same template finds the first true of any monotonic predicate.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) returning the length of the longest substring without repeating characters, using a sliding window and an int[128] of last-seen positions.

checks.label: keeps an int array of last-seen positions
walks the string with a right pointer
moves the left edge but never backwards (max with left)
measures the window as right - left + 1
tracks the best length

questions.explanation: The Math.max(left, ...) is the part people forget: for "abba" the second a must not drag the left edge backwards. A HashMap<Character, Integer> version is equally correct.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int[] slidingMax(int[] nums, int k) returning the maximum of every window of size k in O(n), using an ArrayDeque of indices.
questions.starter:

checks.label: uses an ArrayDeque/Deque
removes smaller values from the back
drops the front index when it leaves the window
adds the current index
reads the maximum from the front once the first window is full

questions.explanation: The deque holds indices whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is always the window maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, hence O(n).

questions.prompt: Match each ArrayDeque call with its effect.

right.text: Inserts x at the front (the top when used as a stack)
Inserts x at the back (the tail of a queue)
Removes and returns the front, throwing if the deque is empty
Reads the back without removing it, returning null if empty
Removes and returns the front, returning null if empty
Sorts the elements and returns the smallest

questions.explanation: The name families matter: push/pop/peek work on the front, offer/poll/peek on the queue ends, and the "poll" and "peek" forms return null while "pop" and "remove" throw.
For a missing key it returns -(insertion point) - 1. The insertion point of 4 is index 2 (before 5), so the result is -3. Test the return value with < 0, never with == -1.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: In Java, int mid = (lo + hi) / 2 can produce a negative mid for very large arrays.
questions.reason: Java int arithmetic wraps around silently when the sum exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE.

whys.a: Correct: lo + hi can exceed 2^31 - 1, wrap to a negative number, and the division keeps it negative. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 or (lo + hi) >>> 1.
whys.b: R is exactly the mechanism, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: I ran it: with lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 the naive form gives -397483648 while the safe forms give 1,750,000,000. The bug was famously present in the JDK binary search for years.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Used as a queue, ArrayDeque is usually faster than LinkedList.
questions.reason: ArrayDeque allocates a node object with prev and next pointers for every element.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the Javadoc says so), but ArrayDeque stores elements in a resizable circular array, not in per-element nodes; the node-per-element design is LinkedList.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The array layout gives better cache locality and no per-element allocation. ArrayDeque rejects null elements; LinkedList accepts them.

questions.text: Declare Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>(); then st.{1}(x) puts x on top, st.{2}() removes and returns the top, and st.{3}() reads it without removing.
questions.explanation: With push/pop/peek the top is the front of the deque, so the printed order of an ArrayDeque used as a stack is top first.

questions.prompt: In modern Java code, java.util.Stack is the recommended class for a stack; ArrayDeque is only for queues.

options.why: java.util.Stack is a legacy Vector-based class with synchronised methods.
Correct: the Javadoc recommends Deque implementations such as ArrayDeque for stack operations.

questions.explanation: Stack extends Vector and synchronises every call. Prefer Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>().

questions.prompt: ArrayDeque does not accept null elements, so adding null throws a NullPointerException.

options.why: Correct: null is reserved as the "empty" return value of poll and peek, so it is rejected on insertion.
It does throw; the check exists so poll() == null can mean empty.

questions.explanation: LinkedList and ArrayList accept null; ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue do not. I ran add(null) on an ArrayDeque and got the exception.

questions.prompt: A Java loop reads while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid; else hi = mid - 1; }. Which situation makes it loop forever?

options.text: a[mid] < target while mid == lo, e.g. lo = 0, hi = 1
options.why: Correct: lo = mid leaves lo unchanged, so the range never shrinks.

options.text: The array contains many repeated duplicate values in a row
options.why: Duplicates change which index is found, not whether the loop ends.

options.text: The target is smaller than every element in the whole array
options.why: hi keeps decreasing until it drops below lo, so the loop exits.

options.text: The array length happens to be an odd number of elements
options.why: Parity does not matter; the update rule for lo does.

questions.explanation: Use lo = mid + 1 for the "go right" branch (or switch to the half-open template). Always check that every branch shrinks the range.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Arrays.binarySearch and Collections.binarySearch are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The input must already be sorted, otherwise the result is undefined.
options.why: Correct: the Javadoc states the behaviour is undefined for unsorted input.

options.text: With duplicate equal elements it does not guarantee which matching index is returned.
options.why: Correct: any index of an equal element may come back.
False: it returns -(insertion point) - 1, which is -1 only when the insertion point is 0.

options.text: On a LinkedList, Collections.binarySearch still makes O(n) link traversals.
options.why: Correct: it uses an iterator-based search, so only the comparisons are O(log n).

questions.explanation: Use lowerBound-style loops when you need the first or last match, and remember the negative return encoding.
